newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU wheat prices swept higher in grain company feud.
newsitem.headline: EU wheat prices swept higher in grain company feud.

text.p: Key European wheat prices jumped this week, driven mainly by export demand as the European Union Commission acted to avert a squeeze on export licences.

The EU Commission, facing growing disarray in a market short of licences, pulled out its biggest export award of the season to prevent at least one company gaining a dominant position in available paper, grain traders and EU officials said.
Traders at the company declined comment.
-- French wheat edged higher most of the week and rode up another five to 10 francs after Thursday's EU decision to release 436,500 tonnes, compared with forecasts of 250,000.
Most traders were gleeful at the EU decision, which followed a tense stand-off between exporters over control of licences.
But they cautioned the market was not yet out of the woods.
"The market is still very nervous and is really taking things vessel by vessel," said one French trader on Friday.
For traffic within Europe, fob Creil French wheat for northern destinations rose in sympathy with the port activity but by Friday buyers were more relaxed, dealers said.
Italy was still a strong outlet for French supplies. Animal feed manufacturers were also dipping into the market.
Traders said that with Rouen-delivered export wheat at 895 francs a tonne, excluding carrying charges, several co-ops were ready to start selling actively once prices reached 900 francs.
Some had already increased their sales this week, they said.

French barley looked fragile despite a strong export award of around 400,000 tonnes, with markets pressured by further declassification of malting barley to feed and the withdrawal of the sole major export buyer om the market on Wednesday.
French maize continued its recent strength on the back of wheat and demand from starchers.
-- Benchmark European prices.
French prices exclude carrying charges of 54.53 francs for first-half march and 58.17 for second half. Italian durum prices are Wednesday's official closes on the Milan exchange.

-- German wheat was also underpinned by shipper demand but the upside was limited by comfortable supplies, traders said.

Turnover was slim and unlikely to pick up in the near future. Fob bread wheat prices (12 percent) had peaked at 280 marks in February and were expected to ease from current levels of 277.50 marks, one said.
Bread rye and oats prices were expected to hold up but those of wheat, barley, maize and triticale were seen easing.
-- Italy's wheat prices were stable to higher, while maize fell as a result of extra foreign crops on local markets.

Durum rose slightly amid rumours of scarce availability of the local Italian crop, but the Italian Institute for Agricultural Studies (Ismea) thought it was unlikely the local crop had all been sold in such a limited amount of time since last summer.
"It is more likely producers are not willing to sell the crop and this could cause an increase in prices," Ismea said.
-- In Spain, dealers said Thursday's move by the EU to aid exports out of Europe was boosting prices, especially of barley which was thought likely to benefit from the move.
Traders said a vessel was loading this week at Valencia.
Durum wheat prices surged amid short supply, they said.
Maize harvesting was now over, and hence prices were gradually weakening.
-- In Britain strong underlying demand meant sterling's rise against other European currencies had little effect.
"The way things are going in the UK, we can use most of the wheat we've got, if not all," one trader said. "There's still a reasonable amount of shipper demand."

But demand from shippers was all for business already booked, another said. "OK, the French market has gone firm in the last few days. It means the UK could do a bit of extra business, but nothing untoward," he said.
"The basis of this market is merchant buying," he said. "Consumers want to take a bit of cover, particularly on April/May/June."
"Farmers have been selling a bit, at their usual level of around 95 stg ex-farm."

One feed compounder buyer disagreed. "People (consumers) are fairly well covered on the nearbys; April, May, June and in some cases July," he said. "In the short term positions most people are fairly well bought up."
"By going forward they're protecting their feed costs at the end of the year."
He reckoned farmer selling was still limited. The response of many traditionally-minded farmers in current circumstances was to "shut the barn door on a rising market."

One knock-on effect of the rise in wheat prices was that buyers were looking again at barley, he said. "At these prices barley starts to look more attractive." Compounders could start putting more barley in mixes.

Ironically, industry sources elsewhere argued, the attempted squeeze play on wheat export licences seemed to have helped the Commission by fuelling demand for surplus coarse grain. Stg 1.00 = $1.6041).
